title: Three weeks of rising pressures
note: Fictional patient. Findings and values are illustrative and follow the module text; your unit’s protocol, the access team and the attending nephrologist decide every order.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on the dialysis rotation of a hospital hemodialysis unit in Lucena City, Quezon. Mr. Romeo Villareal, 61, a retired tricycle driver with diabetes, has dialyzed three times a week through a left forearm arteriovenous fistula (AVF) for two years. Nobody has written an end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) Life-Plan for him, as the Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) 2019 guideline advises.

The nurse, Ms. Joy Abrenica, stops you on the Monday round. His venous pressure alarms have been climbing for three weeks, and after Friday’s session his needle sites bled for 25 minutes. The monthly laboratory sheet shows his Kt/V lower than last month, with no change in the order. The fellow is in the ward; the attending nephrologist rounds at noon.

choices.text: Examine the fistula in order, then put the findings beside the flow sheet.
choices.feedback: Examination localizes the narrowing before any test does. In 142 referred patients, it found outflow stenosis with a sensitivity of 92% and a specificity of 86% against blinded angiography. Trainees on rounds will do less well, but the skill is cheap and available in every province. Look at both arms and the chest, feel for the thrill, raise the arm, do the augmentation test, listen, check the hand.

vitals.exam: Pulsatile; stays full on arm raise; high-pitched bruit

choices.text: Order a repeat Kt/V and a recirculation study, and review the results with the fellow next week before examining anything.
choices.feedback: A falling Kt/V is a real clue, but a laboratory test confirms what your hands can find today. A narrowing keeps growing while you wait a week.
choices.then: The fellow asks you to examine the fistula before the noon round. You go back to the chair.

vitals.exam: Pulsatile; stays full on arm raise; high-pitched bruit

choices.text: Ask the nurse to lower the blood flow so the venous alarm stops sounding, and continue the session.
choices.feedback: That silences the alarm, not the narrowing, and it lowers the delivered dose. The alarm is the access telling you something.
choices.then: Ms. Abrenica asks you to look at the arm first. You examine it.

vitals.exam: Pulsatile; stays full on arm raise; high-pitched bruit

n2.scene: Neither arm is swollen and there are no veins on the chest. The fistula pulses strongly instead of buzzing, stays distended when you raise his arm above his heart, and has a high-pitched bruit. His hand is warm and pink.
n2.prompt: What do these findings point to?

choices.text: Inflow stenosis on the arterial side, near the anastomosis, because the fistula is not delivering enough flow.
choices.feedback: An inflow narrowing gives a weak, flat fistula with poor augmentation and low arterial pressure alarms. His vein is full and pulsatile, and his alarms are venous.
choices.then: The fellow walks you back through the physiology: high pressure upstream of a downstream narrowing.

vitals.exam: Pulsatile, no collapse: outflow narrowing likely

choices.text: An outflow stenosis downstream of the needling segment, given the pulse and the bleeding.
choices.feedback: A narrowing downstream raises the pressure in the vein above it. The vein pulses and will not collapse on elevation. That fits rising venous pressures and longer bleeding after the needles come out.

vitals.exam: Pulsatile, no collapse: outflow narrowing likely

choices.text: A strong pulse means a strong fistula. Document “AVF functioning” and move on to the next patient.
choices.feedback: A pulse in place of a thrill is the sign of a downstream narrowing, not of health. “AVF functioning” hides the finding from the next person who reads the chart.
choices.then: Ms. Abrenica points out the bleeding times on the flow sheet. You look again and rewrite the note.

vitals.exam: Pulsatile, no collapse: outflow narrowing likely

choices.text: Central vein stenosis in the chest, probably from an old catheter.
choices.feedback: Comparing both arms and the chest was right. But central stenosis usually swells the whole arm and opens collateral veins on the chest, and he has neither. The narrowing is more likely in the arm.
choices.then: You re-read your own findings. With no swelling and no chest veins, the arm is the likelier site.

vitals.exam: Pulsatile, no collapse: outflow narrowing likely

n3.prompt: The fellow asks you to draft the referral. What do you write, and what else do you do?

choices.text: “AVF with high venous pressures, for evaluation,” sent to the vascular surgeon as a routine referral.
choices.feedback: It names the problem but not the evidence or the urgency. A referral that joins the trend and the examination gets the patient seen sooner.
choices.then: The fellow rewrites it with the trend and the findings, and agrees the urgency with the attending at noon.

choices.text: Wait for next month’s laboratory results to confirm the trend before referring.
choices.feedback: Three weeks of rising pressures and longer bleeding already are the trend. Act on the trend, not on the clot.
choices.then: At noon the attending asks for the referral today. You write it with the fellow.

choices.text: A one-sentence referral with the three findings, the urgency agreed, and Mr. Villareal told.
choices.feedback: The flow sheet and the examination belong in one sentence. The fellow needs to know who in the province can image or intervene within days and what it costs. The patient needs to know why it matters. “Venous pressures rising for three weeks, bleeding 25 minutes after needle removal, pulsatile fistula that does not collapse on arm elevation.” Use the local imaging pathway.

n4.scene: The family chose to have the imaging on Friday, after payday. Mr. Villareal arrives early on Wednesday and says the buzzing in his arm stopped last night. You feel no thrill and hear no bruit.

choices.text: Try to needle the fistula anyway; if blood comes back, dialyze as usual.
choices.feedback: No thrill and no bruit means no flow: the fistula has clotted. Needling it wastes time that the clot does not give you and can bruise the vein that might still be saved.
choices.then: Ms. Abrenica gets no blood return. You stop and call the fellow and the attending.

choices.text: Do not needle it. Call the fellow and attending now for the fastest declotting pathway.
choices.feedback: Loss of thrill and bruit is a stop-and-call finding. A clotted fistula may not be salvageable if it waits, and the patient goes back to a catheter. A clotted fistula is time-sensitive; the attending decides how he dialyzes today.

choices.text: Ask for a temporary catheter for today’s session, then refer the fistula.
choices.feedback: He may need a catheter, but that is the attending’s decision, and declotting comes first. Every catheter is a bridge that injures the veins it passes through.
choices.then: The attending asks for an urgent declotting attempt before any catheter is placed.

choices.text: Send him home and keep Friday’s imaging appointment, since it is already booked.
choices.feedback: Two more days may be too late for the clot. Thrombosis is time-sensitive, and a call to the attending is the minimum.
choices.then: The fellow sees the note and calls the attending. Declotting is moved to today.

n5.scene: The interventional team cleared the clot and opened a narrowing in the outflow vein. Two weeks later Mr. Villareal is admitted with cellulitis of his foot. The ward team orders a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) in his right arm for a week of intravenous antibiotics.
n5.prompt: The ward resident asks you about it. What do you advise?

choices.text: Hold the PICC and discuss alternatives; sign “save right arm”; write his Life-Plan.
choices.feedback: PICCs injure arm veins and the central veins every arm access drains through. KDOQI considers it reasonable to avoid them in chronic kidney disease (expert opinion). His next fistula depends on what the ward does this week. Dorsal hand veins, or a small-bore internal jugular line if central access is truly needed; the right arm is his next access.

choices.text: Agree to a peripheral cannula instead, rotating sites up the right forearm.
choices.feedback: Better than a PICC, but the forearm cephalic vein is the commonest fistula vein. Use the dorsal hand veins and label the arm.
choices.then: You move the cannula to a hand vein and write the Life-Plan with the fellow.

choices.text: Agree to the PICC in the right arm, since his fistula is on the left.
choices.feedback: The right arm is his next access. A PICC can scar its veins and narrow the central veins it drains through.
choices.then: The fellow cancels the order and asks for a hand vein. You write the Life-Plan together.

choices.text: Suggest the PICC go in the left arm, so the right arm stays clean for later.
choices.feedback: The left central veins carry his working fistula’s outflow. A PICC there risks a central narrowing that swells the arm and ends the fistula. No needles or lines in a fistula arm.
choices.then: The fellow stops the order. A hand vein is used, and you write the Life-Plan together.

end.title: Three months later
end.text: Mr. Villareal still dialyzes through his left fistula, examined in the same order at every round. His chart carries a written Life-Plan: the current access, the right arm as the next one, a note that he and his family have heard about peritoneal dialysis, and a date for the annual review.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Examine the fistula the same way every time: look, feel, raise the arm, augment, listen, check the hand.
  • Pulsatile and does not collapse on elevation means outflow narrowing; weak and flat means inflow.
  • Act on the trend, not on the clot. Put the flow sheet and the examination in one referral sentence.
  • No thrill and no bruit is a stop-and-call finding; do not needle a clotted fistula.
  • Protect the next access on the ward: no PICC without asking nephrology, hand veins for blood draws, and a written Life-Plan.

See Examine the fistula, Dysfunction and Vein preservation.
